170: (40) They are not permitted, etc. - This is a rabbinic enactment because of an incident that occurred, as is found in the Talmud, tractate Chullin 94a "There was an incident involving a man who invited three guests during a famine, and he had nothing to set before them except for about three eggs. The host's son came in. [One of the guests] took his portion and gave it to him. And so did the second [guest], and so did the third. The child's father came and found him holding one [egg] in his mouth and two in his hands. He struck him to the ground, and he died. When his mother saw this, she went up to the roof, fell off, and died. He himself [the father] went up to the roof, fell off, and died." See there. And the commentators Magen Avraham and *Eliyahu Rabba* wrote that this prohibition applies specifically in a case like the one in the Talmud, where the meal was precisely measured and the host would be embarrassed if [food] were missing for them [the guests]. However, if there is plenty on the table such that nothing will be lacking because of this, they are permitted to give to them. According to this, it is certainly permissible if they have already finished eating and some food remains, it is permitted to give them from the leftovers. However, in the book Shemen Rokeach, he is stringent and doubts all of this [and rules it is forbidden].

(41) Or to his servant - Some say that it is specifically forbidden to give to his [the host's] servant, but it is permitted to give to the waiter who is serving the meal. And there are those who say that it is even forbidden to give to the waiter.
